name: Revolax Fine / Deep / Sub-Q

card.summary: A Korean hyaluronic acid filler range in three depth variants, used to smooth fine lines or add volume and contour.
card.note: Injectable procedure by a licensed provider; vascular complications are rare but serious.

quick.overview:
Revolax is a range of hyaluronic acid dermal fillers made by Korea's Across Co., sold in Fine, Deep and Sub-Q versions for different injection depths. They are used to soften lines, restore volume and shape features such as cheeks or jaw.
Hyaluronic acid fillers as a class are well described: results last months and the gel is gradually absorbed.
quick.how: Providers choose the variant by depth, with finer gels for superficial lines and firmer gels for deeper volume. Treatment is a clinic procedure.
quick.risks: Typical effects are bruising, redness and swelling; infection, lumps and allergic reactions are less common, and vascular blockage can rarely cause permanent vision loss. Regulation differs by country.

lead: Revolax is a family of hyaluronic acid injectable fillers from Across Co., offered as Fine, Deep and Sub-Q variants for different treatment depths.

Hyaluronic acid is one of the most common filler materials and is used for facial wrinkles and folds, volume loss, and enhancing features such as lips, cheeks and jawline.[1] Wikipedia says lighter gels are used for superficial injections and firmer products for deeper structural support.[1]
Looksmaxxing forum threads mentioning sub-q injections concern injection sites generally rather than this product.

chain: Inject HA gel at an appropriate depth
angle.text: The depth-specific gels let a provider target fine lines or deeper contour. Results are temporary because the gel is reabsorbed.

paras: HA fillers are usually cross-linked with chemicals such as BDDE to improve stability, since natural HA breaks down quickly.[1]

Common effects include bruising, redness, pain and itching; infection and allergy are less common, and vision loss from vascular embolization is rare but usually permanent.[1] In the US fillers are FDA-regulated devices requiring a prescribing provider, while in the UK/EEA they are CE-marked non-prescription devices.[1]
No studies have examined this specific product range.
